transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-07 15:00 UTC | Duration 58m | Recording available
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Marta (Redwood CSM), Carlos (Zenbridge CTO), Priya (SRE), Liam (VP Product), Juno (Infra)

[00:00] Ava Thompson: okay thanks everyone for joining, we'll try to keep this tightly focused. main goal is walk through the incident follow-up actions and make sure the next test plan and rollback windows are solid.
[00:18] Carlos Mendez: thanks Ava, appreciate it. last week was, uh, rough. end users saw 5–10x token latency spikes and a handful of 502s. we lost some SLAs and the product team is breathing down our necks.
[00:32] Priya Sharma: overall root was the kv-cache staleness plus a memory bloat path when requests hit a rare long-sequence branch. cache invalidation cascade, basically.
[00:45] Ravi Patel: right, from our end we saw the same pattern; sequence lengths that normally average 400 tokens spiked to 1,600 in a subset of prompts and the kernel selection switched to a heavy allocator path. there was some mis-routing to the small-quant variant as a fallback which then overloaded the queuing layer.
[01:10] Liam O'Connor: can you clarify "fallback to small-quant variant"? why did that happen, shouldn't the routing policy keep the pinned model?
[01:20] Ava Thompson: good question. during the surge the smart routing policy attempted cost-containment and circuit-broke to cheaper variant when latency SLOs looked to be in danger. that policy hit roughly the same time the kv-cache returned empty prefixes so effective compute increased, which triggered fallback heuristics.
[01:43] Juno Park: and that was partly because our request fanout duplicated a handful of calls, so cache hit ratio dropped. there's also a race where multiple nodes invalidated the same prefix.
[01:58] Priya Sharma: transcription note: the invalidation window we ran was 60s; maybe too aggressive for their workload.

[02:10] Ravi Patel: quick timeline recap — 02:15 UTC spike, autoscaler started to kick, then a kernel switch at 02:18 to a path that allocs large pinned buffers, OOMs follow, retries flood, routing flips to small-quant variant, small-quant queues up, and 502s start.
[02:35] Carlos Mendez: that matches our timeline.

[03:00] Ava Thompson: right — so the mitigation plan we recommended yesterday: 1) disable routing fallback for critical routes, 2) bump cache invalidation grace to 5m for the problematic prefixes, 3) deploy the KV-cache fix that dedupes invalidation events, and 4) run a controlled canary with lowered concurrency. any concerns with that order?
[03:24] Priya Sharma: step 2 (increase grace) feels risky for data correctness, some prompts rely on stale safety tokens. we need to scope which prefixes are safe to extend.
[03:35] Liam O'Connor: agreed. product side can't have stale safety tokens on billing flows.
[03:41] Ravi Patel: understood — we should separate prefixes: safety-related prefixes remain strict; high-volume generative prefixes get extended grace. we can provide a mapping.
[03:55] Marta Li: I'll take owner for mapping and share with Zenbridge by Friday.

[04:05] Priya Sharma: about the KV-cache patch — does it fully eliminate the race or is it a mitigation?
[04:12] Ravi Patel: it's a mitigation that introduces a short distributed lock for invalidation and de-dupes invalidation events. it reduces but does not 100% guarantee against the race in pathological failure modes. we think it's enough combined with routing changes.
[04:31] Carlos Mendez: do you have telemetry we can see for the de-dupe?
[04:36] Ravi Patel: yes, we'll share a short kernel-selection trace, and an example KV invalidation dump from a synthetic run. LINK: https://redwood.internal/attachments/kv-dump-sample (redwood internal).

[05:00] Juno Park: operationally, can we get an isolation plan if the canary still causes partial degradation? we'd prefer automatic fallback to isolation rather than global routing flips.
[05:10] Ava Thompson: absolutely — we can set a canary policy that isolates traffic to a dedicated lane and automatically steps down if p50 latency > X or error rate > Y for 5m. that's what Dedicated burst lanes are for.
[05:28] Priya Sharma: what's the expected cost delta for a Dedicated burst lane for the 10% traffic canary? Liam needs numbers for finance.
[05:35] Ava Thompson: rough estimate: 15–25% cost bump for the canary window depending on instance mix; I'll follow up with a tighter number.

[06:00] Carlos Mendez: security questions — we need to see SOC2 evidence and details about the KMS integration; also audit trail for the automatic routing decisions.
[06:10] Marta Li: yes we'll share the security pack. Ava will send SOC2 attestation and KMS notes. LINK: https://redwood.docs/security-pack.pdf
[06:20] Ravi Patel: routing decisions are logged at token-batch granularity. we can provide an audit extract showing why a request was routed to variant X with timestamps and decision rationale.

[06:38] Liam O'Connor: going back to the technicals — can you explain the "heavy allocator path" more simply? is this something in our app prompts we can avoid?
[06:46] Ravi Patel: it's primarily triggered by sequences with large attention spans — think long dialogues with many embedded system messages. if you can reduce unnecessary context or compress system tokens, it reduces the chance of hitting that kernel. but it's not always possible for product flows.

[07:10] Priya Sharma: we also saw memory fragmentation on nodes after the surge. Garbage didn't compact quickly and the next allocations failed. is there a recommended JVM or runtime tweak?
[07:21] Ravi Patel: pointer — in our runtime we recommend turning on slab allocators and enabling the new compacting allocator in the kernel for these workloads; we'll include exact flags in the trace doc. but note that some OS images have buggy compaction so test in staging.

[07:50] Carlos Mendez: any chance the model itself produced pathological long sequences because of an eval change?
[07:55] Priya Sharma: product changed a template last week that added verbose system guidance for edge-case prompts; we'll audit that.

[08:10] Ava Thompson: okay let's go through the proposed test plan, sequentially:
 - Day 1: Deploy KV-cache dedupe patch to staging, run synthetic spike with capped concurrency, collect kernel traces.
 - Day 2: Map prefixes and adjust invalidation grace on non-safety keys.
 - Day 3: Run 48-hour soak with canary traffic (10%) routed to Dedicated lane with strict isolation.
 - Day 5: Review soak signals, decide to roll to prod or rollback.

[08:55] Juno Park: can we compress Day 1/2 to accelerate? the business needs this faster.
[09:02] Ava Thompson: we can parallelize some steps — Ravi can push the patch while Marta coordinates prefix mapping. but soak needs time; 48 hours is minimum to catch slow leaks.

[09:18] Ravi Patel: note: during synthetic runs we'll log per-prompt sequence length distribution, kernel selection, cache hit ratio, and the routing decision stream. we'll give you a one-page TL;DR and the raw traces.

[09:32] Priya Sharma: good. for rollback window, we want a plan that doesn't require full database rollbacks. can we rely on routing policy flips as an emergency off switch?
[09:42] Ava Thompson: yes, we can configure a manual or automatic global route to a stable model variant with warmed KV cache; that's our emergency shield. but warm-up latency may be higher for cold caches.

[10:00] Carlos Mendez: what's the expected impact to user experience during a protective routing flip?
[10:06] Ravi Patel: you'll see a moderate quality delta on some prompts — a 2–3% drop in relevance for certain structured outputs in our benchmarks, and token latency improvement. tradeoff is quality vs availability.

[10:30] Liam O'Connor: product will accept a small quality dip for 15 minutes if it means no 502s; we prefer that.

[10:40] Marta Li: note for follow-up: we'll prepare a communication template for incident comms if canary fails and we need to do an emergency routing flip.

[11:00] (long technical interlude where Ravi reads kernel traces)
[11:10] Ravi Patel: you can see at trace 0x3d2 the allocator jumps from 32MB to 512MB per-token buffer because of attention window size, that is expensive. there's also duplicated invalidation events at 02:17:42 which coincide with autoscaler spin-up.

[11:40] Carlos Mendez: those duplicated invalidations — are they coming from multiple nodes or from the same controller?
[11:46] Ravi Patel: looks like multiple nodes tried to assert the invalidation after a partial failure; race due to lack of leader election for that prefix. the patch adds simple compare-and-swap to avoid multiple writers.

[12:02] Priya Sharma: will compare-and-swap introduce more latency in the critical path?
[12:08] Ravi Patel: negligible for the common case, worst-case adds 5–10ms on invalidation events which are rare relative to token time.

[12:30] Juno Park: can we also change autoscaler thresholds? it currently scales reactive to CPU which is noisy for these models.
[12:36] Ava Thompson: recommend switching to an adaptive policy based on request-latency and queue-length signals combined; we can share recommended thresholds.

[13:00] (background crosstalk)
[13:12] Carlos Mendez: question: if the fallback to small-quant caused the queuing cascade, would pinning the model fix that without other changes?
[13:20] Ravi Patel: pinning helps but it doesn't solve the root allocator spike — if the main model is starved of GPU memory you'll still see failures. pinning just avoids quality/regret from fallback, but you still need cache/invalidation fixes and autoscaler tuning.

[13:45] Priya Sharma: ok let's record decisions so we have clear owners.
[13:50] Ava Thompson: decision list: (1) disable automatic fallback for critical billing and safety routes (owner: Carlos/Priya), (2) deploy KV-cache dedupe patch to staging (owner: Ravi), (3) create prefix mapping for extended grace (owner: Marta), (4) run 48h canary in Dedicated lane (owner: Zenbridge ops + Redwood), (5) prepare communication and rollback playbook (owner: Marta).

[14:25] Liam O'Connor: timeline expectations?
[14:28] Ava Thompson: we think we can get patch + mapping and a first canary within one week if parties move quickly. the soak is 48h after that.

[14:40] Priya Sharma: finance wants an estimate of worst-case Dedicated cost for the 48h soak. Ava you'll send the ballpark and Ravi will include the instance mix.

[15:00] Ravi Patel: one more technical ask: can Zenbridge provide the set of prompts that produced extremely long sequences? we can run them through a quantized offline run to see if model truncation or prompt design is the root cause.
[15:12] Priya Sharma: we'll export a redacted bundle with examples and drop in shared staging bucket.

[15:25] Carlos Mendez: for audit, can you include routing decision logs in the post-run package? product wants to be able to show auditors why we routed or didn't route.
[15:33] Ravi Patel: yes we'll include the routing audit extract.

[15:48] (brief pause)
[16:00] Marta Li: next steps recap — I will send meeting notes and the prefix mapping template, Ava will send security pack and pricing, Ravi will share KV dump + kernel traces, Priya will validate staging patch, Carlos will provide prompt bundle. We will meet again 2026-04-20 to review soak.

[16:30] Carlos Mendez: thanks everyone. one ask — after the soak if things look good we want a two-week gradual rollout, not big bang.
[16:38] Ava Thompson: agreed, we'll propose a phased rollout plan in the soak review.

[16:50] Liam O'Connor: thanks.
[16:55] (meeting ends)

Post-call notes (auto-generated): Summary: incident caused by KV-cache invalidation races + allocator path triggered by long sequences; fallback routing amplified the problem. Primary mitigations: dedupe invalidation patch, selective extension of cache grace, disable auto-fallback for critical routes, Dedicated canary. Action items assigned as above.

References and attachments: LINK: https://redwood.internal/attachments/kv-dump-sample, LINK: https://redwood.docs/security-pack.pdf, LINK: staging-bucket/zenbridge/prompt-bundle (Zenbridge internal).

Transcription imperfections: speaker labels occasionally merged (e.g., Ravi/Ava), some proper names mis-recognized, timestamps approximate.
